summary: Defines the base SMIng language, a protocol-independent data definition language for management information. Separate documents map it to protocols such as SNMP. It is experimental and not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: A new way to write down the list of things on a device that can be watched or changed, meant to work with many tools.

subtitle: A protocol-independent language for describing management data, recorded as an experiment after the IETF effort closed.

tldr.problem: SMIv1 and SMIv2 are bound to SNMP, and the SPPI is bound to COPS-PR. Even though the languages share many rules, it is hard to use common data definitions with both protocols.
tldr.mechanism: SMIng defines management information as classes with attributes and events, grouped into modules, using a set of base types such as integers, octet strings, enumerations, bit sets and pointers. Separate documents map the language to specific protocols such as SNMP.
tldr.outcome: The IETF SMING Working Group was closed down in April 2003 without consensus on SMIng or the rival SMI-DS. This memo and the SNMP mapping were published for the record of the NMRG's work.

today: RFC 3780 is an Experimental RFC, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It was published to record the NMRG work after the IETF SMING Working Group closed without consensus.

sections.title: Why SMIng Exists
sections.content:
Traditionally, management information is a set of managed objects in a virtual store called the Management Information Base (MIB), written in a language called the Structure of Management Information (SMI). SMIv1 and SMIv2 are bound to SNMP and based on adapted subsets of ASN.1. Policy provisioning information uses the SPPI, bound to COPS-PR. SMIng aims to be a common data definition language that specifies data models independent of specific protocols and applications.

The RFC records the history. SMIng started in 1999 as a research project to address drawbacks of SMIv2, mainly its partial dependence on ASN.1 and its many exception rules. The work moved to the IRTF Network Management Research Group in 2000, and the IETF SMING Working Group was chartered at the end of 2000. Neither SMIng nor the competing SMI-DS found enough consensus, and the working group closed in April 2003. This memo records the NMRG work for informational purposes.
sections.plainLanguage: Two groups each had their own way of writing the same kind of list, and the lists did not mix. SMIng tried to make one list format for everybody, but the grown-ups could not agree on it.

sections.title: Classes, Attributes and Modules
sections.content:
Management information is modeled in classes. A class can be defined from scratch or derived from one parent class; deriving from multiple parents is not possible. A derived class inherits the parent's attributes and events. Each attribute is an atomic piece of information with a base type, a sub-type of a base type, or another class. A class may also define events.

Related definitions live in modules, identified by upper-case names, and a module can import identifiers from other modules. A module may define classes, events, derived types, identities, and extensions. Every identifier must be unique within its namespace and must not exceed 64 characters. Items must be defined before they are referenced, so there are no forward references, and clashes between imports are resolved with the form Module::item.
sections.plainLanguage: A class is like a form with blanks to fill in, such as an Interface form with a speed blank and a status blank. A module is a folder holding related forms.

sections.title: Types and Language Syntax
sections.content:
The base types are OctetString, Pointer, ObjectIdentifier, Integer32, Integer64, Unsigned32, Unsigned64, Float32, Float64, Float128, Enumeration and Bits. Derived types may restrict the allowed values, for example by size ranges for octet strings. An OctetString has a theoretical limit of 2^16-1 (65535) octets, although the RFC warns of interoperability limits above 255 octets.

An SMIng file holds zero or more modules. Comments start with // and run to the end of the line. A module has its meta information first (optional imports, then organization, contact, description, an optional reference, and at least one revision) followed by extensions, typedefs, identities and classes in that order. The full grammar is given in ABNF in an appendix.
sections.plainLanguage: SMIng has a few kinds of building blocks, such as whole numbers, decimals, text and on-off switches. You can make new blocks by narrowing the old ones, like a number that can only be between one and ten.

sections.title: A Class Example
sections.content: Each attribute states its type, its maximal access (eventonly, readonly or readwrite, from least to greatest), and optionally a default, a format, units, a status and a description. The access value is the maximal level and is independent of any administrative authorization policy. The RFC's example describes an Interface class with read-only speed and operStatus attributes, a read-write adminStatus attribute and a linkDown event.
sections.plainLanguage: Each blank on the form says what kind of answer goes in it, whether you may read it or change it, and what it is for.

sections.title: Revising Modules and Extending the Language
sections.content:
Changes to a module must not risk interoperability problems. A new revision statement goes in front of the earlier ones, the module name must not change, and obsolete definitions must not be removed because other modules may import them. Allowed revisions include adding named numbers to an Enumeration or Bits type, moving a status from current to deprecated or obsolete, and adding attributes to a class. Changing the meaning of a definition requires a new identifier.

The extension statement lets modules declare new statements, optionally with an ABNF grammar, so a parser can complain about unknown or misused statements. The RFC names the SNMP mapping, inlined annotations and annotations to external definitions as possible uses.
sections.plainLanguage: If you change a rule in a shared rulebook, you add a note about the change and never tear out old pages, because someone might still point to them.

sections.title: Security
sections.content: The document defines a language for writing and reading descriptions of management information. The RFC states that the language itself has no security impact on the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: It is only a way of writing things down, so it cannot by itself open any doors for bad guys.
